opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's changed it quite a lot, honestly.

When I started working on language modeling, around the early 2010s, progress felt incremental. You'd spend months getting a small improvement on a benchmark, and the idea that a single model could hold a coherent conversation, write code, or reason through a math problem seemed decades away. A lot of us in the field assumed that kind of capability would need fundamentally new ideas we hadn't thought of yet.

What surprised me was how far some fairly simple ideas could go once you combined them with scale. Pretraining a model on lots of unlabeled text and then adapting it to a task was something we were exploring back then with sequence autoencoders and language model pretraining, and at the time it was a modest trick that helped on classification. Nobody I knew predicted that pushing that same basic recipe, with more data, more compute, and better architectures like the Transformer, would produce what we see today.

So my intuition has shifted in two ways. First, I've become much more humble about predicting timelines. Things I thought were ten years out have happened in two or three, and a few things I thought were close are still hard. Progress isn't linear. It comes in bursts when the right pieces line up. Second, I've learned that the gap between "this works in a research paper" and "this is used by hundreds of millions of people" can collapse remarkably fast once the technology crosses a usefulness threshold.

It's also made me take the responsibility side more seriously. When things move this quickly, you can't assume society will have years to adapt. The research community has to think about safety, evaluation, and deployment much earlier in the process than we used to.

r001.rationale: He contrasts progress that once felt incremental with capabilities and adoption arriving much faster than expected, saying timelines he thought were ten years became two or three and progress comes in bursts.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's recalibrated my whole sense of what "fast" means. I spent years at Google Brain, and back in 2015, 2016, we were excited when a model could write a sentence or two that sort of held together. We'd pass those samples around the office like they were a big deal. And they were, at the time.

But I remember thinking the hard problems, the really interesting ones like long-form reasoning or coherent dialogue over many turns, were comfortably a decade or more away. I had this internal timeline, and I felt pretty confident in it. Then transformers came along, and then scale started doing things nobody had cleanly predicted, and that timeline just collapsed. Things I'd mentally filed under "someday" started showing up in a year, sometimes in months.

So the biggest change isn't really that I think technology moves fast now. It's that I've lost trust in my own intuition about what's far away. When I catch myself saying "that's not happening anytime soon," I now treat that as a signal that I should probably look harder, because I've been wrong in that exact way enough times to be humble about it.

The other thing that struck me is how uneven it is. Capabilities jumped, but a lot of the surrounding work, like making systems reliable, making them safe, figuring out how they fit into people's actual lives, moved at a much more normal, human pace. So you get this strange experience where the frontier is sprinting and everything around it is walking. Living inside that gap is what really changed my sense of speed.

r001.rationale: He contrasts his earlier belief that major AI capabilities were a decade or more away with their rapid arrival in months or a year, describing his timeline as having collapsed.

astra-6.text:
It’s made me more cautious about saying something is a long way off. When you work on AI, you see the incremental progress—the experiments, the things that don’t work—and then occasionally those improvements add up to a capability that feels like a sudden leap. From the outside, it can look almost overnight.

But I also think there are two different clocks. One is how quickly the technology improves, and the other is how quickly people can put it to useful, reliable use. Those don’t necessarily move at the same speed. So I’ve become more open to rapid changes in capability, while recognizing that understanding what those changes mean and integrating them into everyday life can take longer.

r001.rationale: He says he is now more cautious about assuming progress is a long way off, because incremental AI improvements can add up to sudden leaps that look almost overnight from the outside.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s made me realize that progress can feel slow for a long time and then suddenly feel very fast. When you’re working on AI, you see all the limitations and the experiments that don’t work. But those incremental improvements accumulate, and eventually you cross a threshold where the technology becomes useful to a much broader group of people.

So I’ve become more cautious about saying that something is a long way off just because it doesn’t work well today. At the same time, a compelling demonstration and a reliable product are different milestones. You can be surprised by how quickly a capability appears and still underestimate how much work it takes to make it dependable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI progress can feel slow for a long time, then suddenly very fast, and that this changed his perspective.
